What if an AI could keep coding while you’re in meetings? Erik Hanchett’s recent DEV post shows exactly that.

He outlines five reusable patterns—scheduled jobs, persistent memory, sub‑agents, workflow orchestration, and autonomous bots—that let an LLM run as a background worker.

Using the open‑source Kiro Crew harness, a daily Lighthouse audit can run automatically, capture the report, and open a pull request with suggested fixes. Memory files stored as markdown let the agent recall preferences like “Vue.js” or “tabs over spaces” without being reminded each time.

The post also notes that similar capabilities appear in Claude Code, Codex, and OpenClaw, meaning you can experiment with any of these tools today.

Why does this matter? It removes repetitive grunt work, freeing developers to focus on design, testing, and performance‑critical tasks.

A small caveat: running multimodal models in visual comparison workflows can increase token counts and cost per run, so budgeting is needed.
